body_html:
A Road in Bloom, or Un camino en flor in Spanish, is the first bilingual book I published, and the one closest to my heart. It holds 300 short truths about love, family, friendship, money and the slow, quiet work of growing up, written in English with natural Spanish woven right into the sentences. After ten years of translating between English and Spanish, I wanted to write the kind of book I wish I had been given as a learner: not a grammar textbook, but something worth reading even if you didn’t care about the Spanish at all. This is the story of why I wrote it, what you will find inside and how I hope you will use it.

The book at a glance
  • Title: A Road in Bloom | Un camino en flor
  • What it is: 300 bilingual truths about love, peace and growing up
  • How it works: short English pages with key Spanish phrases placed right beside the English, plus a Spanish Note on how the language really works
  • Length: 304 pages, published in November 2026
  • For: adults who already know some Spanish and want to read something meaningful in it, a little every day
{{toc}}

Why I wrote A Road in Bloom

For years, my job has been to move meaning from one language to another. When you do that every day, you notice something: words stick when they are attached to something that matters. Nobody remembers el lápiz está en la mesa, the pencil is on the table. People remember the Spanish they heard in a hard conversation, in a love letter, at a family dinner, in a moment that meant something.

Most Spanish materials I saw went the other way. They taught correct sentences about nothing in particular, and they treated learners as if they had no inner life. I wanted to do the opposite: start with the things adults actually think about, like relationships, boundaries, self-worth, money, family and peace, and let the Spanish grow out of those thoughts.

That is where the idea of a book of “truths” came from. Each page is a short reflection, the kind of sentence you might underline, send to a friend or think about on the way home. The Spanish is woven into it, so you learn the language in the same moment you feel something.

What you will find inside

A Road in Bloom is organized around the big themes of growing up, the ones that never really finish:

  • Love and relationships: what it means to love well, and to be loved well.
  • Family: the people who shaped us, and the patterns we choose to keep or let go.
  • Friendship: the friends who stay, the ones who drift, and why both are part of life.
  • Money: the quiet ways money shapes our choices, our stress and our freedom.
  • Peace and boundaries: learning to say no, to rest and to protect your energy.
  • Growth and self-worth: becoming someone you are proud to be, slowly.

None of these are lessons from above. They are things I have learned, often the hard way, and written down as simply as I could, so that a reader can take one page and carry it through the day.

{{image:2}}

How a page works

Every page in A Road in Bloom follows the same simple pattern, so you always know what to do:

  1. A short truth in English, written to be read slowly.
  2. Key Spanish phrases placed right beside the English, so you see how the same idea sounds in Spanish without having to look anything up.
  3. A Spanish Note, a few lines on how the language really works: an idiom, a false friend, a regional difference or the grammar behind the phrase.

To give you an idea of the kind of thing a Spanish Note explains, here is an example in the same spirit. English has one way to say “I miss you”. Spanish has two common ones: te extraño, which you will hear across Latin America, and te echo de menos, which is the everyday phrase in Spain. Both are correct, and choosing the one your listener uses makes you sound much closer to them. That is the level of detail I care about: not rules for the sake of rules, but the small choices that make Spanish feel natural. (I wrote a full guide to {{link:how-to-say-i-miss-you-in-spanish|how to say I miss you in Spanish}} if you want more.)

Why bilingual, and not all in Spanish

People sometimes ask me why the book isn’t written entirely in Spanish. The answer comes from how we actually learn. You learn a language fastest when you understand almost everything you read and meet just a little that is new. Linguists call it comprehensible input; I explain it in plain English in {{link:comprehensible-input-spanish|comprehensible input for Spanish}}.

When the English carries the meaning, the Spanish has room to land. You are never lost, never reaching for a dictionary every second line, and never reading a sentence so hard that you stop caring what it says. Seeing the two languages side by side also shows you exactly where they differ, which is where most mistakes live. That is the idea behind {{link:parallel-text-reading|parallel text reading}}, and A Road in Bloom is built on it.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Who this book is for

I wrote A Road in Bloom for adults, and especially for:

  • Learners who know some Spanish and are tired of textbooks, but not ready for novels.
  • People in bilingual relationships and families who want Spanish for real conversations about feelings, not just ordering food.
  • Heritage speakers who understand more than they speak and want to reconnect with the language in a gentle way; I wrote more about that in {{link:heritage-spanish-speakers|my guide for heritage Spanish speakers}}.
  • Anyone who likes short, reflective reading, one page at a time, with a cup of coffee.

It is probably not the right first book if you are a complete beginner looking for grammar drills and exercises. It is a reading companion, not a course.

How I suggest reading it

The book works best slowly. My suggestion:

  1. Read one page a day, first in English, then looking at the Spanish beside it.
  2. Read the Spanish phrases out loud. Your mouth remembers what your eyes forget.
  3. Copy one phrase you like into a notebook or your phone, and use it once that day, even in a text message. This is the habit I describe in {{link:sentence-mining-spanish|sentence mining}}.
  4. Come back to the pages that stay with you. The second reading is where the Spanish really settles.

Ten minutes a day with a book like this does more than an hour once a week. The Spanish has time to sink in between sessions, and the reflections have time to mean something.

{{image:3}}

The title: a road in bloom

I chose the title because growing up never felt like a straight line to me. It feels more like a road you walk slowly, where things open up a little at a time: a lesson you finally understand, a relationship that becomes healthier, a version of yourself you start to like. Learning a language is the same. You don’t wake up fluent; one day you just notice that something has bloomed. Un camino en flor is my way of saying that both journeys deserve patience.

The other two books

A Road in Bloom was the first of three bilingual books, and the other two follow the same format with different themes. {{link:love-slowly|Love, Slowly}} (Amor, despacio) is about crushes, heartbreak and choosing yourself. {{link:the-mind-lies|The Mind Lies}} (La mente miente) turns to psychology: overthinking, habits, fear and why we think, feel and act the way we do. You can read them in any order; each one stands alone. For a broader look at how to choose and use books like these, see {{link:bilingual-books-for-adults|bilingual books for adults}}.

A last word

If you read A Road in Bloom, I hope one page stays with you longer than you expected, and that a few Spanish phrases come with it. That is all I really wanted: a book that helps your Spanish and your life grow a little, at the same time. If it does, I would love to hear about it. You can find me on Goodreads.

faq.q: What is A Road in Bloom about?
faq.a: It is a bilingual book of 300 short truths about love, family, friendship, money, peace and growing up, written in English with natural Spanish woven in and a Spanish Note on how the language works.

faq.q: Is A Road in Bloom good for beginners?
faq.a: It is best for learners who already know some basic Spanish. Complete beginners looking for grammar exercises may want a course first.

faq.q: Is the book written entirely in Spanish?
faq.a: No. Each page is written in English with key Spanish phrases placed beside it, so you always understand the meaning while you learn the Spanish.

faq.q: How long is A Road in Bloom?
faq.a: The paperback has 304 pages. It was published in November 2026.

faq.q: Where can I buy A Road in Bloom?
faq.a: It is available on Amazon. You can find the link in the book box on this page.
